He followed close behind my wandering steps;
And when at night the door closed on our room,
His little paw touched mine through the bars of hope.

author: cushag
text: When I left school at eighteen or so, I went home and told my mother that I had got a situation as clerk in a big house—the house where Mr. Fuddles lived. She cried because she was frightened for me, but said nothing about what she thought, which was that I ought never to have left school. All I knew was that they were going to pay me fifteen shillings a week, including supper and lodging, and that my room would be next door to Miss Lizzies. So I put on my new suit (which father bought me), took off my old clothes

“There is no use,” said I, “of your talking so.”

The day is coming when the grass will be fire,
When the trees are all on end, as if they were dying.
They will burn up, like a crop that has been sown.
Then no leaf will fall till spring shall come again,
Till then we must not make any fires at night.

author: emily_dickinson
text: I have often thought it must be rather odd to see a man and his wife quarrelling with each other. It has been my practice in such cases to walk away from them quietly ; but as their disputes are generally carried on in loud voices, they soon follow you, and ask what business you had there; to which I answer that their quarrel concerns me no more than their love does; and then I walk off again. This course may appear singular to some people ; nevertheless, when once a husband gets out of temper with his wife, he seldom will allow himself to return till she repents

We feel as if we were done.

author: cushag
text:
" O ma lord," said Molly Murphy,
" An' ye be sure to do me right ;

Ye must remember that we love each other,

I be no more than half a day dead.

When yer father went to heaven,
He left my mother behind;

So, ma lord, make me like her,

To be happy without you here !"

Of beauty and delight.
There are no bounds for joy, nor end to love,
Nor limit to delight.

 When first she turned and saw him;
 Did he imagine that they two
 Should stand alone together?
 For evermore before their eyes
 Was scattered gold upon the wind,
 But still his song went up to God,
 The Lord of love and life.

This is a little rhyme we wrote;
 For every bee that flies,--
 For ever and aye, as long as time
 Shall run its course or dies.

How many do we find today?
 Tell me, good reader, pray!

author: john_masefield

I'm on my way down-town; I see our house
Across the street, I hear the wind complain
As it blows off Lake Michigan. Its tone is slow
But not so still as if it had gone home.
All around me are sounds from cars and trains,
From ships at sea, and people talking lanes.

The river murmurs, as it flows from out
Its rocky bed; while on the bank, where first
It spreads its bosom, greening lawns, and woods
With whispering shade, invite him far to wander;
Or, if he please, he may pursue the flood
To some wild streamlet whose clear waters gleam
Along their rocky beds in sparkling streams,
Till lost at last in marshy pools beneath
Oft-heard are sounds of night-birds, and coy-foxes' barkings,
Or still soft moans of crickets.

One had a brain like steel, but he did not care.
The other lived for others all his life through--
He loved them very dearly, even to despair.

There is no need that I should mention what befell him:
His son grew up in wickedness and sin;
So after many troubles, at last they met again;
The one full grown, the other old and blind."

Has moved away this week; we heard no good-bye.
It came as though he had fallen asleep in bed,
Or left the house on business and forgot to return."

"Now here we are in summer weather,
On top of our great work and toil;
We're nearly through, no more to fear,
And yet this man—so very slow!
Oh God! He is so full of folly,
With notions as wild as a crow!'
His thoughts he keeps all in his head,
Like one who never looks outside.

The sun was shining on the sea.
 The sky was clear and blue;
 And all things dried up perfectly
 Since the water-rat had gone to sea.

Once I was walking on a country road
 And saw a cow grazing peacefully;
 At the sight I turned my steps and stood
 To watch its placid movements more closely.
 Suddenly it lifted up its head as if listening for something,
 Then with an open mouth bared its teeth at me,
 And suddenly rushed towards me
 Without turning either right or left.
 That is how we humans are too.

O Soul! who hast thy feet upon this shore,
Whose vision from beyond hath led thee there :
The world that thou dost gaze upon before —
Thou mayst not, now, look back and see no more.
But ah ! if at this moment thou should’st know
Some friend or kinsman fallen beneath a sword ;
Then, lift thine eyes again, and mark how low
The sun declines, to set him from thy view.

Before I died;
To have my last desire
Granted, if God were good enough to let it be!
The time was short, for fear
Of death might keep me near;
And yet a little while
Might spare a sight of all that I loved most dearly.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
The Night-Piece of a Lover


In this dark hour (my Dear!) when Fancy paints
 All Nature into passion—when the heart,
 As from its prison-house of fleshly parts,
 Flutters in air, impatient for release—
 When night has spread around us all her wings,
 And we are lost together in the deep,
 By day forgot, among these starry hills
 Of the unknown world, which no foot hath trod
 Since first our Maker made them—in such hours
 We hold communion, when the world grows still,
 The stars move

The night comes on, and from a starless sky
 A shadow flits--a shadow like no shade.
 So beautiful she was once known in pride,
 And now no more is seen. Her name was Trade.
 But still, alas! to us she lives, we live
 By her--by her our hopes are bound--and why?
 Because without her all our happiness
 Has ceased to exist. She went away
 To England long ago. We thought no more
 Of her or loved her less for being gone.
 What care we if she were lost? Why

author: william_wordsworth
text:
In this fair Island, when the sun begins
 To gild the mountains, o'er whose purple tops
 The mists are rising like delicious fumes,
 And all their snowy summits brightly glows,
 From out the clouds we see, where they repose,
 Those stars which in our hemisphere appear,
 Which make so beauteous an aspect here,
 That 'tis the only part of heaven they want,
 To grace it with eternal brightness more.

author: william_wordsworth
